words.definition: To use humor and irony to expose and criticize people's foolishness or vices.
words.example: The cartoonist loves to satirize politicians by exaggerating their worst habits.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'satyr-ize' — picture a mocking satyr poking fun at the powerful and proud.

words.definition: Sharp, cutting remarks that mean the opposite of what they say, used to mock.
words.example: 'Oh, great job,' she said with such sarcasm that everyone knew she was furious.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'sarkazein,' to tear flesh — biting words that tear at you.

words.definition: Fond of joking; playful and good-humored in speech or manner.
words.example: His jocular tone at the funeral surprised the mourners, who expected solemnity.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'jocus' means joke — a jocular friend keeps the jokes coming.

words.definition: Playfully witty or mischievous, given to droll and teasing humor.
words.example: The waggish student answered every quiz question with a clever, teasing pun.
words.mnemonic: A dog's tail 'wags' happily — a waggish person wags a mischievous wit.

words.definition: Delivering humor or remarks with a blank, expressionless, and utterly serious face.
words.example: She delivered the joke deadpan, never cracking a smile, so half the room missed it.
words.mnemonic: 'Dead' face + 'pan' (old slang for face) = a lifeless, unmoving face.

words.definition: Scornful laughter or contempt directed at someone considered worthless or foolish.
words.example: His wild plan met only derision from investors, who laughed him out of the room.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'rision' (laughing, as in 'risible') — laughing someone down.

words.definition: Teasing, insulting behavior or speech meant to make someone seem foolish or ridiculous.
words.example: The other children's mockery of his accent made him afraid to speak in class.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'crockery' — imagine someone smashing your fine crockery while laughing at you.

words.definition: A comic performance that mocks something serious through absurd exaggeration and imitation.
words.example: Their burlesque of the royal wedding replaced the crown with a plastic bucket.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'burla' meaning joke — it turns a serious thing into a joke.

words.definition: A light comedy full of ridiculous, improbable situations, or an absurdly mismanaged event.
words.example: The trial became a farce when the judge fell asleep and the witness fled.
words.mnemonic: French 'farcir' means to stuff — a play stuffed with silly, over-the-top chaos.

words.definition: So absurd and chaotic that it seems ridiculous rather than serious.
words.example: The meeting turned farcical when three managers argued for an hour over the coffee order.
words.mnemonic: 'Farce' + '-ical' — belonging to a farce, so laughably ridiculous.

words.definition: So foolish, unreasonable, or out of place that it deserves to be laughed at.
words.example: Paying a thousand dollars for a plain white T-shirt seems utterly ludicrous to me.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'ludere' means to play — something so playfully silly (think 'ludo') it's laughable.

words.definition: Wildly unreasonable, illogical, or so senseless that it seems impossible to take seriously.
words.example: It's absurd to expect a toddler to sit silently through a three-hour opera.
words.mnemonic: 'Ab-surd' — from Latin 'surdus' (deaf/senseless), an idea too senseless to hear out.

words.definition: A quality of being out of place or clashing with what surrounds it.
words.example: The incongruity of a neon sign on a medieval church startled every visitor.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'congruity' (agreement, like congruent triangles) — things that don't fit together.

words.definition: Seeming to contradict itself while possibly still being true or making sense.
words.example: It's paradoxical that spending more on quality boots can actually save you money.
words.mnemonic: 'Para-' (contrary to) + 'dox' (opinion, as in orthodox) — contrary to expected belief.

words.definition: A clever, witty, and often cutting remark made quickly.
words.example: When asked about his rivals, the comedian shot back a quip that had reporters laughing.
words.mnemonic: 'Quip' is quick + zip — a fast, snappy line that zips right out.

words.definition: A remark or action meant to be funny rather than serious.
words.example: He made the outrageous boast in jest, so no one took offense.
words.mnemonic: A jest is what a court JESTER (fool) tells to make the king laugh.

words.definition: Lighthearted, teasing talk exchanged between people in a friendly way.
words.example: The two coworkers traded banter all morning, laughing between tasks.
words.mnemonic: Banter is a light 'canter' — words trotting easily back and forth.

words.definition: Quick, clever replies traded during a conversation.
words.example: Her sharp repartee left the smug heckler with nothing to say.
words.mnemonic: From French 'repartir,' to reply — a fast comeback shoots right back.

words.definition: Playful, carefree behavior that lacks any serious purpose.
words.example: After the exams, the students surrendered to a weekend of pure frivolity.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'free-vol-ity' — free, floating, weightless fun with no weight to it.

words.definition: Not serious or sensible; concerned with trivial, unimportant things.
words.example: The judge dismissed the frivolous lawsuit as a waste of the court's time.
words.mnemonic: Think 'frills' — fussy, unnecessary decoration that serves no real point.

words.definition: Playfully naughty in a charming, harmless way.
words.example: An impish grin crossed her face just before she hid his car keys.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'imp' — a little devil-child forever up to small tricks.

words.definition: Fond of causing playful trouble or minor annoyance.
words.example: The mischievous puppy unrolled the entire roll of toilet paper.
words.mnemonic: 'Mis-chief' — a little chief in charge of small misdeeds.

words.definition: Playfully dishonest or mischievous in a charming, likable way.
words.example: He gave a roguish wink as he slipped the last cookie into his pocket.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'rogue' — a charming rascal or lovable scoundrel.

words.definition: An insulting or mocking remark meant to taunt someone.
words.example: The rival fans hurled gibes at the losing team as it left the field.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'jab' — sharp words that jab at you to sting.

words.definition: To argue or complain about a small, unimportant detail.
words.example: Let's not quibble over who pays the tip; the meal was wonderful.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'nibble' — nibbling away at tiny, petty points.

words.definition: Showing quick, clever humor in speech.
words.example: Her witty toast had the whole wedding roaring with laughter.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'pretty' — a pretty clever line that lands just right.

words.definition: A ridiculous person who behaves in a foolish, clownish way.
words.example: The class buffoon balanced a spoon on his nose to get a laugh.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'baboon' — a clownish ape making a fool of itself.

words.definition: Silly, clownish behavior that seems ridiculous or is meant to amuse.
words.example: The teacher had no patience for the buffoonery disrupting her lesson.
words.mnemonic: 'Baboon-ery' — the ridiculous antics of a clowning baboon.

words.definition: A wild, playful, or absurd act intended to amuse.
words.example: The children's bedtime antics kept the babysitter chasing them for an hour.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'antico' — the grotesque, clowning figures painted in ancient Roman ruins.

words.definition: A playful leap, or a lighthearted, mischievous adventure.
words.example: The heist turned into a comic caper when the alarm simply would not stop ringing.
words.mnemonic: Think Capricorn the goat — it capers about, leaping and frolicking.

words.definition: A loud, hearty, and sudden burst of amusement expressed out loud.
words.example: When the clown slipped on the banana peel, the whole audience erupted in a guffaw.
words.mnemonic: Sound it out: 'GUH-FAW!' — a bellow so loud it shakes the room.

words.definition: To laugh in a breathy, gleeful, half-suppressed way that shows satisfaction.
words.example: She chortled with delight as she unwrapped the exact gift she'd been hinting at for weeks.
words.mnemonic: Coined by Lewis Carroll from 'chuckle' + 'snort' — a chuckle that ends in a snort.

words.definition: To laugh quietly and slyly, often in a mocking or disrespectful way.
words.example: The students snickered behind their hands when the teacher's toupee slipped sideways.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sneaker' — a sneaky, sneaker-quiet laugh you try to hide.

words.definition: To give a short, nervous, partly suppressed laugh, often from embarrassment.
words.example: A nervous titter spread through the courtroom when the witness admitted he'd forgotten his own address.
words.mnemonic: 'Titter' echoes the 'twitter' of birds — high, fluttery, nervous little sounds.

words.definition: To laugh in a loud, harsh, shrill way, like a clucking hen.
words.example: The witch stirred her cauldron and let out a shrill cackle that echoed through the forest.
words.mnemonic: Picture a hen after laying an egg — that harsh clucking IS the sound.

words.definition: Deserving to be mocked or laughed at; absurdly ridiculous.
words.example: His risible excuse — that aliens had eaten his homework — earned only a raised eyebrow.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ridere' (to laugh), the same root as 'ridiculous' — if it's ris-ible, you can't help it.

words.definition: A person fond of making clever jokes or mischievous witticisms.
words.example: Some wag in the back office had taped a googly-eyed photo over the boss's stern portrait.
words.mnemonic: He 'wags' his tongue nonstop with jokes, like a dog wagging its tail.

words.definition: A light, humorous imitation that mocks something by exaggerating its features.
words.example: The comedy troupe's spoof of the spy thriller had the hero tripping over his own gadgets.
words.mnemonic: 'Spoof' sounds goofy — a goofy send-up of something serious.

words.definition: An absurd or inferior imitation that grossly distorts and debases its original.
words.example: The rushed trial was a travesty of justice, over before the defense could call a single witness.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'travestire' (to dress across) — a serious thing dressed up in absurd, unfitting clothes.

words.definition: Cheerful, merry, and lighthearted in mood or manner.
words.example: In a jocund mood after the good news, he whistled all the way home and tipped everyone twice.
words.mnemonic: 'Jocund' ~ 'joke' + 'fun' — shares its root with 'jocular.'

words.definition: Marked by loud noise and laughter, or so funny it provokes them.
words.example: The stand-up set was so uproarious that patrons were pounding the tables and gasping for breath.
words.mnemonic: 'Uproar' + -ious — an UPROAR of noise and merriment.

words.definition: Boisterous merriment, or an outburst of amusement and cheer.
words.example: The dog stole the sausages mid-barbecue, and the ensuing chaos dissolved the guests into hilarity.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'hilaris' (cheerful) — the same root behind 'hilarious.'

words.definition: Amusing in a way that causes people to smile or laugh.
words.example: The penguin's comical waddle across the ice made even the grumpiest visitor grin.
words.mnemonic: 'Comical' ~ 'comic' — like a comic-book gag or a comedian's bit.

words.definition: Puzzled, confused, or lost in mild bewilderment.
words.example: She stared at the assembly instructions with a bemused frown, unsure which end was up.
words.mnemonic: 'Be-' + 'muse' — so lost in musing you're confused; NOT the same as 'amused.'

words.definition: Showing an offhand, dismissive lack of proper concern for something important.
words.example: His cavalier attitude toward the safety rules alarmed the new lab technicians.
words.mnemonic: A cavalier (horseman) sweeps past on his high horse, breezily dismissive of those below.

words.definition: Free from worry or concern; showing a light, breezy indifference to what might trouble others.
words.example: She gave an insouciant shrug when told the deadline had moved up, as if nothing could rattle her.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-SOO-see-ant' — picture someone 'in a suit, ain't' bothered by anything.

words.definition: Confident, stylish, and charming in a smooth, refined way, especially describing a man.
words.example: In his tailored tuxedo he moved through the party looking utterly debonair, greeting each guest with an easy smile.
words.mnemonic: 'De bon air' is French for 'of good air' — a man with a good, gracious air about him.

words.definition: Lacking liveliness, flavor, or substance; offering nothing that stimulates interest or thought.
words.example: The talk show filled an hour with vapid chatter about celebrities, leaving viewers no wiser than before.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'rapid' but is its opposite in spirit — a 'vap' of flat, stale air with nothing in it.

words.definition: Naive and simplistic, or so dull as to feel empty and unsatisfying.
words.example: His essay offered only jejune slogans, the kind of reasoning a thoughtful reader outgrows by high school.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'juvenile June' — childish, unripe thinking that never matured past its first month.

words.definition: Warm, friendly, and pleasant in manner, putting others at ease.
words.example: Our genial host kept refilling glasses and drawing shy guests into conversation until the whole room felt like old friends.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'genie' — a cheerful genie who grants your wish with a warm smile.

words.definition: Excessively bright, showy, or ornate in a way that lacks good taste.
words.example: The casino's gaudy carpet clashed with neon walls and gold statues, overwhelming the eye at every turn.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'gawdy' — so loud and flashy it makes you gawk and mutter 'oh gawd.'

words.definition: Flattering or praising someone excessively to win favor, often in a servile way.
words.example: The new intern's fawning compliments to the boss made everyone else in the meeting cringe.
words.mnemonic: Picture a young deer (a fawn) trotting after you, adoring and desperate for approval.

words.definition: A clever, amusing remark made in passing.
words.example: He couldn't resist a quick witticism about the burnt toast, and the whole kitchen burst out laughing.
words.mnemonic: 'Wit' + '-icism' — a small unit of wit, like an 'ism' you can toss into conversation.

words.definition: Good-natured teasing or joking directed at someone in a friendly spirit.
words.example: The old teammates greeted each other with rounds of raillery about who had aged the worst.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rally' — friends rally to tease each other, all in good fun.

words.definition: Light, playful conversation exchanged for amusement.
words.example: Their first date was two hours of easy badinage, neither wanting the clever back-and-forth to end.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bad in a garage' — imagine two mechanics trading witty jabs while they work.

words.definition: Referring to sex or the body in a coarse but humorous way.
words.example: After a few drinks Uncle Joe launched into ribald jokes that turned Grandma's ears bright red.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'rib-bald' — jokes that jab your ribs and are baldly, shamelessly crude.

words.definition: Humorously coarse or indecent, especially about sex.
words.example: The tavern rang with bawdy sea shanties that would have scandalized any respectable parlor.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'body' — jokes all about the body, told loudly and shamelessly.

words.definition: Playfully mischievous in a charming, impish way.
words.example: With a puckish grin, she hid everyone's left shoe and waited to watch the confusion unfold.
words.mnemonic: Named for Puck, the trickster sprite in Shakespeare's dream who delights in harmless mischief.

words.definition: Amusingly odd and wildly unconventional in behavior or style.
words.example: The zany inventor showed up with a hat that dispensed spaghetti, insisting it would change breakfast forever.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'brainy' gone sideways — a 'Zanni' clown from old Italian comedy, all antics and chaos.

words.definition: Given to joking; playful and humorous in tone or intent.
words.example: The professor's jocose asides about his own bad handwriting kept the lecture from ever feeling dry.
words.mnemonic: Think 'joke' + 'verbose' — someone whose speech is full of jokes.

words.definition: Inclined to find trivial faults and raise petty objections at every opportunity.
words.example: The captious reviewer circled every comma but never once mentioned the brilliant argument underneath.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'capture' — from Latin capere, 'to seize'; a captious person seizes on your tiniest flaw to complain about.

words.definition: Extremely careful about small details of conduct, etiquette, or correct procedure.
words.example: He was so punctilious about the place settings that a single misaligned fork could ruin his evening.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'punctual' plus the Latin punctum ('point') — someone precise down to the very point.

words.definition: Quick to become annoyed and prone to sharp, spiteful, snappish remarks.
words.example: One waspish comment about her cooking, and she stung him with a whole week of icy silence.
words.mnemonic: Think of a wasp: it stings fast and sharp — a waspish person snaps at you with stinging words.

words.definition: A humorous play on words sharing similar sounds or multiple meanings.
words.example: When the baker called his job 'a piece of cake,' the whole room groaned at the pun.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'fun' — a pun is wordplay meant to be fun, even when it makes you groan.

words.definition: A playful, fanciful quality, or a sudden and capricious idea.
words.example: On a whimsy, she painted her front door bright turquoise and strung wind chimes across the porch.
words.mnemonic: Blend of 'whim' and 'flimsy' — a light, flimsy passing whim that flits through your head.
